fields.meta_title: Coming Soon Page: Examples and How to Build One | Emergent
fields.meta_description: A coming soon page holds your domain until launch. See four real examples, how to keep it indexable and where every signup should go.
fields.h1: Build a Coming Soon Page That Fills Your Launch List
fields.hero_description: Describe what is launching and when. Emergent builds the coming soon page with its countdown and signup form, plus the table where every email lands, on your own domain.
fields.features_heading: What a Coming Soon Page Needs Behind It
fields.features_subheading: Visitors see one small screen. The list behind it and the switch on launch day decide whether the page pays off.
fields.feature_1:
A countdown tied to your launch date

Pick the launch date and time zone once, and the countdown runs to that minute. At zero the page switches to the live site, or shows a short Now open message you wrote.
fields.feature_2:
Signups in a database you own

Every email typed into the page becomes a row in a database table you own, stamped with the time it arrived. Export the list as a CSV, or sync it to your email tool over its API.
fields.feature_3:
A page search engines can index

Serve the page with a 200 status and a real title. Google considers pages that return that status for indexing, and your brand name can appear in results before launch.
fields.feature_4:
One launch email, sent on the day itself

Email the whole list once on launch morning, or hand the list to the email tool you connect. Each message carries a postal address and an unsubscribe link, as CAN-SPAM requires.
fields.feature_5:
Copy and dates changed by message

Ask Emergent to push the date back a week or rewrite the headline, and the page updates at the same address. Signups already in the table stay put through every edit.
fields.feature_6:
Code you keep after launch

Export the full code for the page and its signup table to your GitHub on paid plans. Host it on Emergent under your custom domain, or deploy it beside the product after launch.

fields.tab_content_1:
Twelve days out and 1,240 emails on the list

With its grinder 12 days from shipping, Fernway's domain shows a countdown, the $189 price and one email field. Each signup is saved with the link it came from: 610 from Instagram, 430 from the newsletter and 200 from a podcast ad. On launch morning the whole list gets one email.
fields.tab_content_2:
Who gets a free loaf on opening day?

Halden Bakery's second shop opens on Pine Street, and its coming soon page shows the address and the opening week. The first 50 people to sign up get a free loaf on opening day. Signup 51 learns the loaves are claimed and can still leave an email for opening-day news.
fields.tab_content_3:
Keep bookings coming in while the new site is built

Patients still need appointments while Ridgeway Physio rebuilds its site over six weeks. The coming soon page in its place keeps the clinic's phone number, its hours and a booking request form working. Each request reaches the front desk by email with the patient's name and a preferred day.
fields.tab_content_4:
Chapter one lands in every new reader's inbox

Readers who sign up on Iris Calloway's coming soon page for her second novel get chapter one by email once they confirm. The form also asks which format they plan to buy. So far 312 picked the hardcover, 488 the ebook and 150 the audiobook, and her publisher reads that count before setting the print run.

fields.howto_title: How to Build a Coming Soon Page
fields.howto_description: A coming soon page has one job until launch: turn early visitors into a list. The seven steps below follow the order most teams work in, ending with the hand-over to the live site.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Decide what the page must collect
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Put the date in the headline
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Keep the form to one field
fields.howto_step_1_des: Pick the one thing the page should gather before launch: emails for a product, booking requests for a clinic, a format choice for a book. That choice sets the form, and the form sets the columns of the table that stores each signup.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Say what is coming and when in the first line people read. A real date or a countdown gives visitors a reason to sign up today. A vague promise of soon gives them a reason to close the tab and forget the name.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Ask for an email address and nothing more unless the launch needs it. A bakery giving away loaves may want a name for the pickup list; a product drop does not. Each extra field costs signups you never get to see.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Google slows its crawling when a site answers with 5xx errors, and URLs that keep returning them are eventually dropped from the index. A 503 suits a short outage. A page that waits months for launch should answer with 200 and carry real text.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Tag every signup with its source
fields.howto_step_5_des: Store each email next to the utm_source tag from the link that brought the visitor. By launch day you know which post or newsletter filled the list, and where the next round of promotion should go.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Draft the email the list will receive on launch day while the page is still collecting. Under CAN-SPAM it needs a valid postal address and a clear way to opt out. Send it once, on the day itself, and skip the weekly reminders.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Replace it with the live site
fields.howto_step_7_des: When the product goes live, put the real site at the same address, or send the old URL on with a 301 redirect. Keep the signup table: it becomes your first customer list, with the source of every name on it.

plan.angle: The top 10 is galleries (Dribbble, Pinterest, Envato) and template stores (Canva, Wix, GoDaddy), plus a WordPress plugin and Webflow's design post. They sell the look of a coming soon page. Few say what it has to do: keep the domain indexable with a 200 status, put every signup in a list you own, and send one lawful launch email when the date arrives. This page defines it for the AI Overview, then shows four real pre-launch jobs, each with the list behind it.
